I originally had this concern of the licensing being tied to hardware IDs and if I change multiple parts of my computer then my license would be void and I would have to buy a new Windows license. But after reading this FAQ(http://answers.microsoft.com/en-us/insider/wiki/insider_wintp-insider_install/frequently-asked-questions-windows-10/5c0b9368-a9e8-4238-b1e4-45f4b7ed2fb9)), I was relieved to find that my version of Windows can still transfer licensing.

tl;dr of the part I'm talking about:

When I upgrade a preinstalled (OEM) or retail version of Windows 7 or Windows 8/8.1 license to Windows 10, does that license remain OEM or become a retail license?

If you upgrade from a OEM or retail version of Windows 7 or Windows 8/8.1 to the free Windows 10 upgrade this summer, the license is consumed into it. Because the free upgrade is derived from the base qualifying license, Windows 10 will carry that licensing too.

If you upgrade from a retail version, it carries the rights of a retail version. If you upgrade from a OEM version, it carries the rights of a OEM version.

Full version (Retail): - Includes transfer rights to another computer. - Doesn't require a previous qualifying version of Windows. - Expensive

Upgrade version (Retail): - Includes transfer rights to another computer. - require a previous qualifying version of Windows. - Expensive, but cheaper than full version

OEM : OEM versions of Windows are identical to Full License Retail versions except for the following: - OEM versions do not offer any free Microsoft direct support from Microsoft support personnel - OEM licenses are tied to the very first computer you install and activate it on - OEM versions allow all hardware upgrades except for an upgrade to a different model motherboard - OEM versions cannot be used to directly upgrade from an older Windows operating system

What happens if I change my motherboard?

As it pertains to the OEM licenses this will invalidate the Windows 10 upgrade license because it will no longer have a previous base qualifying license which is required for the free upgrade. You will then have to purchase a full retail Windows 10 license. If the base qualifying license (Windows 7 or Windows 8.1) was a full retail version, then yes, you can transfer it.

One big trend I've seen this generation is the push to digital. Digital was an option in the last gen, but this gen it really feels like physical is becoming a hybrid of physical+digital. What I mean is that if you buy a game on disc, there's a pretty good chance that it wasn't finished by the time the disc was printed (Halo MCC), an even better chance that it will require a 3GB - 10GB update to play (Halo MCC, Plants vs Zombies, Payday 2), and another small chance that mandatory (but free) DLC will be implemented in the future (Titanfall). Games are being designed from the beginning with the assumption that gamers will have decent internet access to complete the product, and while that's true for most gamers, it's an inconvenience to some and an impossible barrier to entry for others. If current trends continue I can see a minority of gamers left behind with no alternative. PCs have already left physical media behind, and it looks like consoles are right on their heels.

Definitely, although it does feel like some companies are attempting to phase out disc purely for the fact it cost to much to keep producing. Less constant updates and a game actually worth a 60 to 90 dollar price tag.

Halo MCC for example required a 16GB day one download because they make more money by not printing the large game on two discs, and because they are able to keep working on the game while sending the discs to the printers early. While this maximizes profits it imposes difficulties on gamers in more rural areas who don't have adequate internet access and who need the complete game on disc. Most countries, particularly in the U.S., have a pretty big gap in quality internet access between rural and urban areas, and it's this kind of "aim for the majority" development that leaves less fortunate gamers behind. In urban areas with adequate internet access and ISP competition, a large day one update means you have to wait a while to play your game. In rural areas with poor internet access it means not being able to play the game at all, even with the disc in hand.

Ive got two main points on this:
1.) The consoles are far too underpowered. If they are to last for 5-9 years they are going to hold back gaming as a whole. People talk about optimization as if the XOne and PS4 devs will suddenly discover an arcane formula of revolutionary design alchemy that will let them hit 1080p/60fps solid in just another year. Its not happening, the horsepower isnt there.

2.) The proverbial needle is pushing into the side of the gaming economy bubble and it is on the verge of bursting. AAA games now cost so much to develop that even selling a ton of copies isnt going to satisfy investors any longer. This is why publishers are making such obvious attempts to turn $60 gamers into $120 gamers. Nobody wants to be the first to break that $60 base game price point, so instead they are pushing out cheap, money-grabbing, over-priced DLC, such as ALL the DLC in Batman:Arkham Knight, bullshit "Season Passes" where the seasons have some nebulous un-announced time limit, and obvious DLC delivery systems like Destiny and Evolve.

I dont want the gaming industry to fail, but I want the bubble to burst. Get EA, Activision, Ubisoft, and their greedy ilk to decide its not worth the investment and quit. Let the talent in the indies continue to shine and rise up. And I hope a new hardware manufacturer enters the ring and shocks the world, like Microsoft did with the original XBox.
